Rebab 一名不晚於八世紀已見，是最早的拉弦樂器之一，經伊斯蘭貿易路線傳入北非: The name rebab is found no later than the eighth century, and it is one of the earliest bowed instruments; it spread along Islamic trade routes to North Africa, western and central Asia, Southeast Asia and parts of Europe. The name has never been fixed, and historically and by region it has covered instruments that differ in construction and in whether they are bowed or plucked. The main variants are the long-necked spike fiddle, the short-necked boat-shaped lute and the pear-shaped lute; the last reached Western Europe in the eleventh century as the rebec and influenced some European bowed instruments. The bowed rebab developed in Muslim culture and was long used in Bedouin music; in Iraq it is called the joza, in Persia there is the similarly formed kamancheh, and it is still played in the Indonesian gamelan and in traditional Malaysian ensembles.
Rebab 為弦鳴樂器，多為擦弦，偶見撥弦。來源稱其音色近似人聲，音域很窄，約略: The rebab is a chordophone, usually bowed but sometimes plucked. The source says its timbre is close to the human voice and its range very narrow, a little over an octave; this is the main difference from related bowed instruments such as the violin and the kamancheh. Local forms affect the pitch: the Ahvaz version in Iran is larger, with a range close to the viola da gamba, and the further west one goes the smaller and higher the instrument. The source does not say directly how volume is controlled, but the gamelan version tunes two brass strings in fifths and the horsehair bow is strung loosely, the bowing hand controlling the tension; it is harder to play and can also end a phrase freely after the beat. Its bow is usually more curved than a violin bow, and the instrument is held upright, on the knee or on the floor.

The body may be of wood or half a coconut shell, covered at the front with parchment, goatskin or cowhide; the Indonesian gamelan uses a very thin stretched skin and Malaysia uses cow stomach lining. Finer versions have a metal soundbox, half covered at the front with hammered copper and half with cowhide. There are one, two or three strings, and Indonesia uses brass strings; the Indonesian bow is of horsehair. The materials of the neck, the tuning pegs and the damping device are not stated.

The rebab, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321-71, is a chordophone, and the name covers several related bowed or plucked instruments found in North Africa, western and central Asia, Southeast Asia and parts of Europe. The common long-necked spike form has a membrane-covered soundbox joined to a long neck and pegbox, with no fingerboard; it is held upright on the leg or on the floor and bowed with a more curved bow than a violin's. Forms and playing methods vary from region to region, and it can be used in Arab Bedouin music, for ornamenting the melody in the Indonesian gamelan, and in traditional Malaysian ensembles and ceremonies.

持琴時，長頸擦弦型多直立，底部尖腳或端柱可抵地或置於腿上；琴身小圓、前蒙皮、無指: The long-necked bowed type is mostly held upright, with the spike or endpin resting on the ground or on the leg; the body is small and round, covered with skin at the front and without a fingerboard. It is sounded with a bow more curved than a violin's and can also be plucked. The gamelan version tunes two brass strings in fifths and the horsehair bow is strung loosely, the bowing hand controlling the tension; a beginner first fixes the position of the body and the path of the bow, then works on the intonation of the stopped notes. In the ensemble two are used, one for pelog and one for slendro, not playing in unison, and a phrase can end freely after the stroke on the great gong.
